summary: Gale Atlas is an interactive Marswalk planner for Namib Dune in Gale Crater. It brings orbital terrain and Curiosity’s surface observations into one place so users can compare routes, plan suit reserves, and make a simulated go / no-go decision. The map shows why the shorter route crosses the dune exclusion zone and how the detour avoids it. Users can also explore historical weather, replay the May 2024 solar storm, and inspect evidence about water ice and seismic activity. By showing the evidence behind each check and where the data has gaps, Gale Atlas lets users see how each choice affects the plan.
details:
From a map to a mission plan

Gale Atlas addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. We built a browser-based tool for planning a simulated walk to an observation stop near Namib Dune.

1. Choose a route

Compare the direct crossing and a detour on HiRISE imagery, contours, a slope layer, and Curiosity’s archived track. The direct route crosses about 44 m of the mapped dune exclusion zone. The detour is about 259 m round trip and has a peak grade of 13.3°. A linked elevation profile and 3D terrain view let users inspect the route before making a choice.

2. Check the return budget

Enter walking speeds, time at the stop, delays, and suit reserves for oxygen, carbon dioxide removal, battery, and cooling. The planner shows which resource reaches its reserve first, how much time remains, and when the crew must leave the stop.

3. Make the go / no-go call

The readiness panel combines terrain, suit reserves, historical weather, radiation, and seismic context. Each result links back to the evidence. A shareable link records the settings so another person can review the same plan.

Science and limits

Explore Curiosity’s Gobabeb sand observations, compare surface and orbital measurements of the May 2024 solar storm, and review regional ice evidence, MOXIE results, and InSight marsquakes. The weather and radiation observations come from historical records. The route, suit inputs, and decision thresholds are illustrative and do not represent NASA flight rules.

How we built it

We used Next.js, React, CSS, SVG, Canvas, and Three.js for the interface. Python and Node.js scripts prepare the archived data and terrain layers. The project repository includes the source code, data preparation scripts, and a methods page with citations and coverage limits.

OpenAI Codex assisted with the interface redesign and code changes. The mission observations come from the cited archives.
